claim_text: The outage ran about 24 hours, Nov 12 to 13
summary: Microsoft puts the outage window at 4:20 PM UTC on Thursday, Nov 12 (11:20 AM ET) to 4:10 PM UTC on Friday, Nov 13 (11:10 AM ET), under incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821.
detail: Third-party copies: Microsoft's own copy of the report needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required). The university mirror shows the same end time in Microsoft's final status text, but its record header lists a 10:05 AM UTC start for EX1550543; we use the report's 4:20 PM UTC.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: Microsoft's preliminary post-incident report gives these incident start and end times.

claim_text: Microsoft's first public notices
summary: Microsoft first posted about Teams problems in North America at 10:40 AM ET on Nov 12, and about Exchange Online mailbox access problems in the Americas at 12:54 PM ET.
detail: Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft's official status account posted the Teams investigation notice at this time.

claim_text: Exchange Online email took the main hit
summary: Most users could not reach their Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook or other mail apps, and email delivery was delayed. Parts of Copilot, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive that rely on Exchange were also affected.
detail: Exchange Online took the main hit: most users could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook or other mail apps, and email delivery was delayed. Parts of Copilot, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Defender and Purview that rely on Exchange Online were also affected. Third-party copy of Microsoft's report; see c001.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The report's User Impact section describes the primary and secondary impact in these terms.

claim_text: Problems reported in at least 70 countries
summary: BBC News reports that Microsoft's email, Teams and Copilot were inaccessible in at least 70 countries, based on outage-tracker reports.
detail: Based on outage-tracker reports. AP reported more than 70 countries from Downdetector data, but its page blocked our check.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: BBC News reports Microsoft's email, Teams and Copilot were inaccessible in at least 70 countries.

claim_text: Microsoft's preliminary report: three factors together
summary: Microsoft's preliminary report blames three things together: a latent defect from a July update to its networking gateway servers, extra load after a Teams failover, and nearly 14% of gateway capacity already out of service.
detail: According to Microsoft's preliminary report, three things together caused the outage: a latent defect in a July update made for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers, extra load after Teams failed over to the same gateway about 15 hours earlier, and nearly 14% of gateway capacity already out of service for an unrelated reason. This is Microsoft's own analysis. A third-party copy of Microsoft's final report, dated Nov 20, gives the same account and adds peak North American traffic as a fourth condition (c020). A Microsoft executive vice president posted a public summary of the same findings on X, reported by ABC News and The Verge.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The report's Root Cause section lists these three factors.

claim_text: More than 80% of gateway servers were unresponsive
summary: Microsoft's preliminary report says more than 80% of the gateway servers were unresponsive at the lowest point, and that safeguards between regions did not stop the failure from spreading worldwide.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The report states both points in its Root Cause section.

claim_text: Microsoft said it was not related to cyber activity or AI
summary: Microsoft said the outage was "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents", introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced by a recent network change.
detail: Microsoft also sent the statement to BBC News, and it appears in the final status text of both incidents. Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft's official X account posted this statement on Nov 13.

claim_text: No sign of malicious activity, Microsoft said during the outage
summary: During the outage, Microsoft's status updates said there was no indication or evidence of malicious or cyber activity.
detail: Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft's official status account said there was no indication the outage was the result of malicious or cyber activity.

claim_text: Engineers investigated and ruled out an attack
summary: Microsoft engineers looked into possible attack routes, consulted DDoS specialists, and ruled out an attack using crash reports and logs.
detail: Single outlet with unnamed sources.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The Verge reports this from sources familiar with the response.

claim_text: The outage was a cyberattack, hack or DDoS
summary: The US government says the recent outages were not a cyberattack, and Microsoft says this one was a technical issue. No independent forensic report has been published.
detail: Also contradicted by Microsoft (c007, c008). No independent forensic report has been published; this label will be revisited if new official findings appear. The White House quotes the Director of National Intelligence saying the recent outages are not a cyberattack, and the Secretary of State saying there is zero evidence any of them involve hackers or hostile actors and that the Microsoft incident is unrelated to the FAA's.
label: Debunked
why_it_supports: The White House quotes the Director of National Intelligence saying the recent outages are not a cyberattack, and the Secretary of State saying there is zero evidence any of them involve hackers or hostile actors.
notes: Microsoft's final report says the same (c021).

claim_text: It was caused by AI-written code or AI agents
summary: People outside Microsoft wondered whether careless AI coding was to blame. Microsoft says the outage was not related to AI or agents; no one else has addressed it.
detail: Microsoft says the outage was not related to AI or agents (c007), and its preliminary report blames a July fix without saying how it was written. Not labeled Debunked because only Microsoft has addressed it. Microsoft's final report also says the change behind the outage was not caused by AI tooling (c021).
label: Rumor
why_it_supports: The Verge reports people outside Microsoft wondering whether the outage came from a cyberattack or careless AI coding.

claim_text: It was part of a coordinated attack with the FAA and bank outages
summary: The White House says officials see no indication of a coordinated cyberattack, and the Secretary of State says the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with the FAA's.
detail: This is the US government's account, not an independent technical analysis. NBC News also reports security researchers saying the simpler explanation is brittle systems.
label: Debunked
why_it_supports: The White House says officials see no indication of a coordinated cyberattack, state-sponsored activity or malign actor, and the Secretary of State says the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with the FAA's.

claim_text: Phishing emails posed as outage notices
summary: Criminals sent phishing emails posing as Microsoft 365 outage notices and falsely warning that held mail would be deleted. Microsoft says stolen credentials and malware have not been confirmed.
detail: Criminals sent phishing emails posing as Microsoft 365 outage notices that cited the real incident ID EX1550543 and falsely warned that held mail would be deleted. Microsoft says stolen credentials and malware have not been confirmed. This was a separate, opportunistic scam that exploited the outage. It did not cause the outage. Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes the campaign, its subject lines and sender domains.

claim_text: Microsoft extended its email timeout to 48 hours
summary: Microsoft extended its email timeout to 48 hours so that mail delayed during the outage would not be returned as undeliverable.
detail: Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft's official status account posted the 48-hour extension.

claim_text: A preliminary report was released inside the admin center
summary: Microsoft released a preliminary post-incident report on Nov 15 to 16, available only inside the Microsoft 365 admin center.
detail: We did not log in to read it. The text we cite is a third-party copy (c001). Labeled Reported, not Confirmed: its official source is a post on a social account, which the site's rules treat as a lead, and it does not have two independent sources besides.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Microsoft's official status account said the preliminary report was available in the admin center under MO1550821 and EX1550543.

claim_text: The final report is due Nov 20
summary: Microsoft's preliminary report says the full list of repair items will come with its final report, due Nov 20, 2026.
detail: On Nov 20 at 8:04 PM ET, Microsoft's service health records for both incidents showed a new notice that a post-incident report had been published. A third-party copy of a report dated Nov 20 is now public (c020), and GeekWire reports that Microsoft released its final report on the evening of Nov 20. Microsoft's own copy needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required).
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The preliminary report's repair-items table lists the full list of repair items as due 11/20/2026 with the final report.

claim_text: Azure's status page showed no events on Nov 18
summary: On Nov 18, Microsoft's Azure status page showed no active events, and Azure's status history listed no incident review newer than Sep 30, 2026.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The Azure status page read "There are currently no active events" when we checked.

claim_text: A major Azure outage happened on Nov 18
summary: We found none. Azure's status page showed no active events, and no outlet we found reported a major Azure outage that day.
detail: Third-party outage trackers showed only scattered user reports on Nov 18. The Microsoft outage people discussed that week was this Nov 12 to 13 Microsoft 365 outage.
label: Not established
why_it_supports: Microsoft's Azure status page showed no active events, and we found no outlet reporting a major Azure outage that day.

claim_text: Microsoft posted a new post-incident report notice on Nov 20
summary: At 8:04 PM ET on Nov 20, Microsoft's service health records for both incidents gained a new notice: "A post-incident report has been published." A third-party copy of a report dated Nov 20 has since appeared (c020).
detail: Seen on a university mirror that copies Microsoft's service health notices but not the reports themselves. The first such notice, at 11:47 PM ET on Nov 15, came with the preliminary report. Microsoft's own copy needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required). Labeled Reported: it rests on one third-party copy, and the notice does not itself say the report is the final one.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: The mirror's records for EX1550543 and MO1550821 each show a second "A post-incident report has been published" notice, timed 01:04 UTC on Nov 21 (8:04 PM ET on Nov 20).

claim_text: Microsoft's final report: a July defect, set off by three conditions together
summary: Microsoft's final report, dated Nov 20, blames a latent defect in a July update to its gateway servers, set off by capacity lost to planned maintenance, a Teams failover and peak North American traffic.
detail: The report says the defect caused lock contention inside an internal Windows process that used up the servers' CPU and memory. It hit only newer servers with more cores, and load testing on older hardware missed it. The defect does not apply to standard Windows deployments. Nearly 14% of gateway capacity was out of service for planned maintenance. At 1:07 AM UTC on Nov 12, a routing issue in the US East region moved Teams traffic worldwide onto the gateways Exchange Online uses. Compared with the preliminary report (c005), the final report names the maintenance as the reason for the missing capacity and adds peak traffic as a condition. This is Microsoft's own analysis. Microsoft's own copy needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required). GeekWire, an established outlet, reported on the final report on Nov 21 and gives the same account, including the July defect, the newer high-core servers, the 14% capacity lost to routine updates and the US East Teams routing issue. KIRO 7, a Seattle TV newsroom, also reported on the final report on Nov 21, quoting its line that Microsoft's testing "did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident". Neowin, an established tech news outlet, reported on the final report on Nov 22 with the same account: a July 2026 defect, reduced server capacity and extra Teams traffic set off a cascade that left more than 80% of the gateway servers unresponsive at one point. The Guardian, in a Nov 22 explainer on the recent run of outages, gives the same outline: an upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lay dormant for months until a string of coincidences triggered it and overwhelmed Microsoft's servers. The Register reported on the final report on Nov 23 with the same account: a July change affecting Microsoft's gateway configuration, not standard Windows, load tests on older lower-core hardware, and more than 80 percent of North American gateway servers unresponsive at the worst point. The Seattle Times also reported on it on Nov 23, describing the July bug, the 14% of servers out for updates and the Teams traffic shift. (The Seattle Times notes that Microsoft Philanthropies underwrites some of its journalism projects.) Next, an established French tech outlet, compared the two reports on Nov 24 and gives the same account, with four factors: the July defect, capacity out for planned maintenance, the Teams traffic shift and peak North American traffic.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The report's Executive Summary and Root Cause sections name the defect and the three conditions; GeekWire, KIRO 7, Neowin, The Guardian, The Register, The Seattle Times and GEroundtable report the same account.

claim_text: Microsoft's final report says it was not a cyberattack
summary: Microsoft's final report says the incident "was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack", that Microsoft found no evidence of malicious activity, and that the change behind it was not caused by AI tooling.
detail: The report also says no enterprise email was permanently lost and customer data at rest was not affected; some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days expired. This is Microsoft's own finding, not an independent forensic report. Microsoft's own copy needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required). GeekWire quotes the same lines from the final report. KIRO 7 also reports that Microsoft has maintained the outage was not related to a cyberattack or AI agents. The Seattle Times (Nov 23) quotes the same line and the AI-tooling statement, and says that as of Nov 23 there was no indication the Microsoft, FAA, JPMorgan Chase and Apple disruptions were related. The Register (Nov 23) reports the final report's account that some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes inactive for more than 30 days expired with non-delivery reports, while all queued enterprise messages were delivered. Next (Nov 24) also reports that the final report explicitly says it was not a cyberattack and that the changes were not produced by AI.
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The report's Executive Summary says the incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack; GeekWire and The Seattle Times quote that line, and GEroundtable, KIRO 7 and The Register report the same.

claim_text: Some email security checks were weaker during the outage
summary: Microsoft's final report says that during the outage, Safe Links may have offered users a "Skip verification" option, depending on their organization's policy, and that post-delivery email protection (ZAP) was delayed.
detail: The report says users may have had trouble opening links protected by Safe Links, and that ZAP, which removes harmful messages after delivery, may not have acted as quickly as usual because updated threat information was not available. This describes protections working less well during a technical outage. It does not say anyone took advantage of it, and we found no report that anyone did. Next, an established French tech outlet, reported both points from the final report on Nov 24. Microsoft's own copy needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login (not checked: login required).
label: Confirmed
why_it_supports: The final report's list of effects on Microsoft Defender for Office 365 names the Safe Links "Skip verification" option and the ZAP delay; Next reports the same two points.

claim_text: Microsoft declared an internal "Code Red" after the outage
summary: Reuters reported on Nov 24 that internal Microsoft memos it reviewed declare a "Code Red" drive to change how the company prevents and responds to major service failures after the Nov 12-13 outage.
detail: Per Reuters, one memo calls the outage the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online. Another says responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to keep a single picture of what was happening. The memos describe five workstreams, including load shedding, splitting traffic by region and faster recovery, and a goal of resolving future worldwide incidents within an hour. Microsoft has not published the memos. A company spokesperson responded to Reuters without disputing them. The same Reuters report repeats that Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents. Ars Technica and The Verge reported the memos citing Reuters. Labeled Reported: it rests on one outlet's review of documents that are not public.
label: Reported
why_it_supports: Reuters says it reviewed the internal memos and quotes them; it also quotes a Microsoft spokesperson responding to the report.
